paras: The killing of Barney Cleveland was the fatal shooting of a Black barber from Moline by a special officer at Milan on August 7, 1880, while the officer was trying to arrest him. Cleveland died two days later, and a coroner's jury found the shooting a justifiable homicide by an officer in the discharge of his duty. The Rock Island Argus followed the case closely and defended the officer, while denouncing local Republicans whom it accused of making Cleveland's race a partisan issue at the inquest.

According to the Argus, Cleveland had lived in Moline for many years, had a large family, and was "a good barber" with "a good trade" when sober. The same report called him "a terror" when drunk and listed earlier arrests in which officers in Moline and Rock Island had beaten or clubbed him and one had his thumb bitten.

On the morning of August 7 a party of Black residents of Moline went to Milan to fish, but Cleveland, the Argus said, left the group and went along Main street, where he became "boisterous and unruly" and fought with James Alexander of Rural. In the Argus account, Special Officer Lever ordered him to stop, called on Robert Keeler and others for help, and was answered with curses and thrown rocks, one of which grazed Keeler. After warning that he would shoot, the officer fired twice when a rock nearly struck his head, hitting Cleveland in the stomach and the lower abdomen about noon near the Milan House.

A Davenport dispatch to the Chicago Tribune gave a shorter version in which Cleveland "picked up a rock" as the officer tried to arrest him and was shot twice; it timed the shooting to the evening. Cleveland was "taken in" badly wounded and died at about 1 a.m. on August 9.

Coroner Morris opened an inquest at 8:30 that morning before a jury of five Republicans and one Democrat, after "self-styled friends of the deceased" objected to Democrats being seated. The coroner cut off one witness who offered opinions as well as evidence, and the Argus reported that the testimony so far favored the officer. Late that day the jury found that Cleveland died "from the hand of Policeman S. H. Leever while in the discharge of his duty" and returned a verdict of justifiable homicide, which the Argus said the community received "with much satisfaction."

No report of any arrest or further prosecution appears in the coverage. On August 26 the Argus reported that Cleveland's widow was living in a one-room shanty in Moline with nine children, the eldest seriously ill, and appealed to "good people in Moline" to help.

All of the coverage found came from white newspapers, and most of the detail came from the Rock Island Argus, which gave the officer's side as fact under the headline "Probable Fatal Shooting." The Argus called Cleveland "the pugnacious negro" and "wickedly devilish" when drinking, and wrote that "Public sentiment is with the officer." Its report of the inquest, headed "A Despicable Attempt to make Political Capital out of the affair," attacked "small minded Republicans" in Milan for trying to create partisan feeling "because Cleveland, the dead man, was colored."

Beyond the Rock Island area the story ran only as a brief, and the Chicago Tribune of August 8 printed both the Davenport dispatch and a one-line item saying Cleveland, "a colored man," was "shot dead" at "Milan, Ia." while resisting arrest. That one-line item was copied into crime digests in the Mower County Transcript of Minnesota on August 12 and the Union County Courier of Dakota Territory on August 18. No Black-press coverage of the shooting was found.

The Tribune brief and the digests reported Cleveland killed on the spot, whereas the Argus, which followed the case daily, reported that he survived until August 9. The Davenport dispatch and the briefs placed Milan in Iowa, while the Argus treated it as part of its own county near Moline and Rock Island without naming a state. The officer's name appears as Lever, Leber and Leever in the Argus, the last in the text of the verdict.

accounts.label: Rock Island Argus (officer's side)
accounts.gist: Cleveland, drunk and unruly, fought a man from Rural, refused the officer's orders, and threw rocks at him and his helpers; after warning that he would shoot, the officer fired twice when a rock nearly struck his head.

accounts.label: Davenport dispatch
accounts.gist: A police officer trying to arrest Cleaveland shot him twice in the lower abdomen when he picked up a rock.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Cleveland died of revolver wounds from Policeman S. H. Leever acting in the discharge of his duty; justifiable homicide.

accounts.label: Friends of the deceased (as described by the Argus)
accounts.gist: They objected to Democrats on the inquest jury, and one witness offered opinions against the officer; their version of the shooting is not reported.

framing.detail: The Argus called Cleveland 'a terror' when drunk and a 'pugnacious negro', said 'Public sentiment is with the officer', and called the attempt to raise partisan feeling over his race 'despicable and reprehensible'.
The Chicago Tribune ran a short Davenport dispatch headed 'Shot by an Officer' and a one-line brief saying he was shot 'while resisting arrest'.
Western weeklies reprinted the brief in crime digests titled 'Recent Tragedies' and 'Bloody Deeds'.

versions.value: Critically wounded Aug. 7, died about 1 a.m. Aug. 9

conflicts.note: The local Argus, which followed the case daily, is the better evidence; the 'shot dead' brief anticipated the death.

versions.value: Treated as local to Rock Island and Moline, 'in the county'; no state named

conflicts.note: The Iowa placement comes from a Davenport dispatch; the Rock Island, Ill., paper's local framing suggests Illinois but does not state it.
